rows.source: Federal Reserve H.6 (via FRED, billions of dollars)
European Central Bank BSI dataset (billions of euro → USD at today's rate)

Bank of Canada Valet API — M0 (notes in circulation + settlement balances of Payments Canada members, from the Bank's own balance sheet, not seasonally adjusted), M1++, M2, M3 (gross, seasonally adjusted); millions of Canadian dollars. Canada has no officially published "M0" aggregate — this is the standard central-bank-money construction (currency + bank reserves), the same definition this board applies to the US and euro-area M0 cells.

Swiss National Bank Data Portal — monetary base M0 (banknotes in circulation + sight deposit accounts of domestic banks at the SNB, not seasonally adjusted, from the SNB's own "snbmoba" cube) + monetary aggregates M1/M2/M3 (CHF millions)

Banco Central do Brasil SGS API — série 1788 "Base monetária restrita" for M0 (the Bank's own definition: moeda em circulação e as reservas bancárias, currency in circulation + bank reserves — a single ready-made series, unlike Canada/Switzerland's two-series constructions) + Meios de pagamento M1/M2/M3 (thousands of reais)

Bank of England IADB — M0 (Notes & Coin in circulation, monthly average, + Reserve Balances at the Bank of England, both not seasonally adjusted: the Bank discontinued its own "M0" label in 2006 and replaced it with exactly these two series, published to be read together, matching its own M0 definition of currency + banks' operational deposits at the Bank) + M2 ("Retail M4", the Bank's own parenthetical equivalence for this concept in its M4 documentation — the household/business retail slice of M4 as against wholesale deposits, NOT a classic M1-plus-savings-deposits M2, seasonally adjusted) + M4 (shown in the M3 column: the UK discontinued M1/M2/M3-class reporting in 2006, so M4 is its own broadest published aggregate today, seasonally adjusted); no current UK M1-class series was found — the Bank's own M0 and M4 detail pages define those two but neither defines a current M1; £ millions
Statistics Norway StatBank — base money M0 + monetary aggregates M1/M2/M3 (NOK millions)

People's Bank of China — Financial Statistics Report (July 2026), read by hand from the Bank's own plain-English press release (pbc.gov.cn); no live keyless API confirmed (FRED's IMF-mirrored M2 series stopped updating in 2019-08, and the Bank's own "Money Supply" statistical tables are real .htm/.xls/.pdf files but sit behind a per-month, unpredictably-timestamped URL with no stable series id or listing feed — hand-refreshing periodically off the monthly report, same posture as the Euro area's hand-curated M0). No M3 published. RMB billions.

Reserve Bank of India — Weekly Statistical Supplement: "Reserve Money: Components and Sources" for M0, "Money Stock: Components and Sources" for M3 (M1 has no row of its own there — derived by summing that same table's own component rows: Currency with the Public + Demand Deposits with Banks + 'Other' Deposits with the RBI, the RBI's own textbook M1 definition). Not RBI's DBIE portal (a JS app with no confirmed keyless API) — these are separate, permanent, server-rendered WSS release pages, crawled for the latest release each time. No M2 published (needs post office savings-bank data RBI doesn't report on this cadence). ₹ Crore.

Bank of Japan — "Main Time-series Statistics" CSV exports (stat-search.boj.or.jp/ssi/mtshtml/csv/), not the REST API (real and keyless, but its exact M1/M2/M3/monetary-base FAME mnemonics couldn't be pinned down from its own documentation — these codes were instead found by hand from the Monetary Base and Money Stock pages' own CSV downloads, whose "Series code" header row names them itself). md01 = Monetary Base (M0, Average Amounts Outstanding); md02 = Money Stock M1/M2/M3 (same measure). 100 million yen.

Reserve Bank of Australia — "D3 Monetary Aggregates" CSV (rba.gov.au/statistics/tables/csv/d3-data.csv), already in A$ billion. Supersedes an earlier finding that this table was xlsx-only (a spreadsheet-parsing dependency this stdlib-only fetcher deliberately avoids) — the RBA has since added a genuine CSV export for it. M0 = "Money base" (DMAMMB, not seasonally adjusted — no SA variant is published); M1/M3 use the seasonally-adjusted series (DMAM1S/DMAM3S). No M2 — Australia's own convention skips straight from M1 to M3 (it separately publishes an even-broader "Broad money" aggregate, but M3 is this economy's own real M3, not a substitution the way the UK's M4 is).

Danmarks Nationalbank — table DNMNOGL "Key figures for the MFI sector" on the api.statbank.dk PxWebAPI instance it shares with Statistics Denmark (a different dialect from Norway's SSB PxWebAPI: metadata lives at a "tableinfo" endpoint and the data query is a plain GET with variable-name params, not a POST json-stat2 body — the earlier note's blocker was the wrong request shape, not a missing endpoint). SEKTORNAT pinned to "all sectors domestic and foreign" (the headline total, not a sector breakdown). No M0 published in this table. DKK million.

Statistics Sweden (SCB) PxWebApi — table FM5001, the "Outstanding money supply, SEK millions" content code (as against the table's other content code, 12-month growth rate, which this board doesn't want); M1/M2/M3, sourced from Sveriges Riksbank. The same PxWebApi 1.0 software as Norway's SSB, but M1/M2/M3 live on their own "Penningm" dimension here rather than through ContentsCode directly, so this needed its own small provider (`scb_pxweb`) sharing the same underlying query helper. No M0/monetary-base table found on this API within reasonable effort, despite Sweden's own textbook M0 definition (banknotes and coins held by the public) being real and commonly cited elsewhere. SEK million.

data.gov.sg — the Monetary Authority of Singapore's own "Money Supply" dataset, via data.gov.sg's CKAN datastore_search API (genuinely keyless — an API key only raises the rate limit, it isn't required). Row labels carry leading whitespace for display indentation in MAS's own table (stripped before matching); the latest month is found by parsing every "YYYYMon"-style column id to a real date rather than trusting column order. No M0/monetary-base dataset found on data.gov.sg within reasonable effort (MAS's own Monthly Statistical Bulletin XML endpoint for it returned a 404 when checked directly). SGD million.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand — hand-curated because the ENTIRE rbnz.govt.nz domain sits behind Cloudflare bot protection that 403s any non-browser request, confirmed across four separate page/file paths (the statistics page, the site search, the data-file index, and a direct .xlsx media URL) — Michael downloaded the actual files by hand through a real browser (from the "Data file index" page, rbnz.govt.nz/statistics/series/data-file-index-page — exact per-file URLs pending, to be filled in once confirmed) and Claude read them locally with pandas/openpyxl (a one-off manual-extraction tool, not a fetcher dependency — the automated fetcher stays stdlib-only and can't reach this domain regardless). M0 = table R1 "Reserve Bank Balance Sheet (Annual Report)" (file hr1.xlsx), Deposits (series RBNZ.MRL121, banks' settlement balances) + Currency in Circulation (RBNZ.MRL124) — the standard currency+bank-reserves construction used everywhere else on this board. M1 + M3 = table C50 "Money & credit aggregates (depository corporations)" (file hc50.xlsx): "A. Narrow money (M1)" (series MCA.MDB.M1) and "Broad money (A+B)" (series MCA.MDB.BM, the RBNZ's own headline broadest aggregate — no separate M2 is published). Refresh periodically the same way, same posture as China's hand-curated entry. NZD billion.

The Bank of Korea's ECOS API requires a free registered access key; only a canned demo "sample" endpoint works keylessly, and — confirmed by a live request — it returns no data for a real current query.

Banco de México's SIE API requires a registered access token — confirmed by a live request, which returned "Token inválido" (invalid token). INEGI's own Indicators API (a second, separate Mexican statistics agency) also requires a registered token — confirmed from its own documentation, re-checked 2026-09-09. No genuinely keyless path found for either agency.
The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey's EVDS API requires a registered API key; an unauthenticated request against it returns nothing — confirmed by a live request.

UPDATE 2026-09-09: found a genuinely keyless, no-auth REST API after all — custom.resbank.co.za/SarbWebApi (its OpenAPI spec declares no security scheme at all, confirmed live). But its 4 curated "Money and Banking" snapshot-graph endpoints turned out to be interest rates and CPI, not money supply; the real money-supply codes (MON0100P/MON0200P/MON0300P) were found by guessing off SARB's own MON-prefix pattern — and every one of them is a 12-month %-CHANGE series (M1/M2/M3 y/y), not a level. This board's schema needs LEVELS (native-currency amounts, summed into the totals row and the scarcity chart) — a % change doesn't fit that shape, so nothing was added despite having real, live, keyless data in hand. SARB's own classic series use a DIFFERENT "KBP"-prefixed code scheme (confirmed via its Online Statistical Query tool's own instructions) for level data, and no KBP code for M0/M1/M2/M3 levels could be found within reasonable effort — the interactive query tool itself would need to be driven to reveal one. A real candidate for a future dated follow-up, not a dead end.

The Bank of Israel runs a real, modern, keyless SDMX 2.1 API at edge.boi.gov.il — confirmed live, and its dataflow list even names the exact one wanted ("MAG" = "Monetay Aggregates", their own typo). But its data response encodes each series as a compact dimension-index key (e.g. "3:0:1:2:1:1:0:2") rather than a named code — decoding which key is M0/M1/M2/M3 needs the dataflow's full structure/dimension map fetched and cross-referenced, a genuinely deeper task than every other provider here (all of which return self-describing codes or labels directly in the data response). A real candidate for a future dated follow-up, not a dead end — the API and the right dataflow are both confirmed to exist.

gold.source_note: World Gold Council, compiled from IMF International Financial Statistics reporting; most recent WGC compilation as of early 2026 (Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 reporting round, per-country update cadence varies — several countries report only quarterly or annually). Tonnages are official-sector holdings only — they exclude private and unofficial holdings entirely.
